plain_english: If you're a thinking person, you can't stand things that don't make sense. But if something makes sense to you, you can tolerate it. Physical pain isn't naturally unbearable. Look at the Spartans — they endure brutal whippings because they've convinced themselves the whipping serves a purpose. Even hanging yourself isn't unbearable if you believe it's the logical thing to do. Here's the point: nothing bothers us more than things we see as senseless. And nothing attracts us more than things we see as reasonable.
original_excerpt: To the rational animal only is the irrational intolerable; but that which is rational is tolerable. Blows are not naturally intolerable. How is that? See how the Lacedaemonians endure whipping when they have learned that whipping is consistent with reason. To hang yourself is not intolerable. When then you have the opinion that it is rational, you go and hang yourself. In short, if we observe, we shall find that the animal man is pained by nothing so much as by that which is irrational; and, on the contrary, attracted to nothing so much as to that which is rational.
source_reference: Discourses, How a Man on Every Occasion Can Maintain His Proper Character

plain_english: Think about what price you're willing to sell your will for. If nothing else, at least don't sell it cheap. But maybe greatness belongs to Socrates and people like him. So why aren't more of us like him, if we're naturally capable? Is it true that all horses are fast? That all dogs are good trackers? Just because I'm naturally slow, should I stop trying? I hope not. Epictetus isn't better than Socrates. But if he's not worse, that's enough for me. I'll never be Milo the strongman, but I still take care of my body. I'll never be Croesus the rich king, but I still manage my money. We don't give up on anything just because we can't be the best at it.
original_excerpt: Only consider at what price you sell your own will: if for no other reason, at least for this, that you sell it not for a small sum. But that which is great and superior perhaps belongs to Socrates and such as are like him. Why then, if we are naturally such, are not a very great number of us like him? Is it true then that all horses become swift, that all dogs are skilled in tracking footprints? What then, since I am naturally dull, shall I, for this reason, take no pains? I hope not. Epictetus is not superior to Socrates; but if he is not inferior, this is enough for me; for I shall never be a Milo, and yet I do not neglect my body; nor shall I be a Croesus, and yet I do not neglect my property; nor, in a word, do we neglect looking after anything because we despair of reaching the highest degree.
source_reference: Discourses, How a Man on Every Occasion Can Maintain His Proper Character
